results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 39 prose/list units' outliner summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph (p01-p39 including p22 placed in in-practice); the three introduction callouts match no spec paragraph, as expected for house-format boxes. The p26 summary ('introducing the side-by-side table') is thin but consistent with the paragraph's role of leading into the comparison table.

Two units were marked two_ideas. Progressive Rollout ¶4 (p14): the cadence material qualifies Adyen's account by showing where its record stops, and the spec's controlling idea joins both; this is support, not a second idea. What to Take Away ¶4 (p37): the Larkfield late/wrong months illustrate the 'what gives way' asymmetry and the one-line exercise applies it, as the spec's controlling idea for the part closing declares; one idea with its callback and takeaway.

Every body unit traces to a supporting claim: scene/problem to S2/S5, rollout to S1/S2/S4, migrations to S3/S4, designs to S1/S5, incidents and culture paragraphs to S4 (which explicitly names engineering-culture facts), comparison to S4/S5, in-practice to S1/S3/S5, recovery to S2/S5. Introduction and conclusion units serve their declared functions.

Each quoted source is followed by a sentence stating what it shows ('Those are the claim's three properties', 'A stage bounds the damage and does not remove it', 'An untested rollback is an untested deployment', 'The same three properties are designed in', 'I draw nothing from the absence'); the stage table, designs table and comparison table each have a lead sentence stating their point; figures are introduced with what they picture.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: The May 2027 Upgrade as a Staged Change ¶1
results.finding: Declared relationship is example, carrying over the recommendation that reconciliation after a change is the integrator's job. The section opens with a bare fact about team size; nothing links back to the preceding recommendation or announces that what follows is that recommendation carried out at Larkfield.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: The May 2027 Upgrade as a Staged Change ¶2
results.quote: The first of them, the comparison, runs dark.
results.finding: Declared example/sequence: the first of the four transferable parts. But the preceding paragraph listed the comparison fourth, so 'the first of them' misstates the relationship to the list it carries over; both flow readers stumbled here.

results.draft_locus: Incidents, Postmortems and the Engineering Choices Behind Them ¶2
results.quote: The teams that do those reviews change a shared code base, and both companies have said what it looks like.
results.finding: flow-A marks this section 'unclear' and says the monorepo, language and build-versus-buy paragraphs answer none of the four questions; flow-B also could not place them. The spec intends these as 'the engineering choices that shape its changes', but the draft never says how a monorepo or owned hardware bears on changing a money path, so the section reads as a detour that exists only to feed table rows.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: An Upgrade That Was Finished When It Deployed ¶2
results.quote: The chapter takes the four questions in order.
results.finding: Both readers tried to map sections onto the four questions and found the mapping breaks (the problem section answers none; the incidents section bends the order). The sentence promises a stricter structure than the chapter keeps.

results.draft_locus: Progressive Rollout: Bounding How Much Traffic a Mistake Reaches ¶1
results.quote: The mechanism that bounds the first two kinds of damage has two parts.
results.finding: The previous paragraph says unknown outcomes arise because code is withdrawn mid-request, so readers could not see how a rollout bounds that damage rather than causing it. The draft does not say that bounding exposure bounds how many payments can be left unknown.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: The May 2027 Upgrade as a Staged Change ¶2
results.quote: The first of them, the comparison, runs dark.
results.finding: The four transferable things are listed with the comparison last, then the next paragraph calls the comparison 'the first of them'; both readers had to re-read. Listing them in execution order would fix it.

results.quote: Read together, the five chapters of this part show an asymmetry that none shows alone.
results.finding: The part-level synthesis sits inside the chapter's takeaways and brings in other chapters' facts (7,900 late renewals, 1,840 double charges, K5, K1); then a second part-level close follows the Questions. Both readers lost the chapter's thread and found the part ending split in two around the questions. The split comes from the spec's placement of p37 before p38 and p39 after it.

results.quote: is this chapter's opening case read as a deployment
results.finding: The failure-patterns box names the Version Cliff and 'a team of eleven' before the lead paragraphs introduce either, so the reader meets references they cannot resolve yet (flow-A also notes the Phantom Payment is never named again in the body).

results.draft_locus: Progressive Rollout: Bounding How Much Traffic a Mistake Reaches ¶2
results.quote: A progressive rollout as Stripe described it in 2024
results.finding: The figure caption dates the source 2024 while the text consistently says 'Stripe's 2023 annual letter (published March 2024)'; both readers stopped to check whether these were two sources.

results.draft_locus: Progressive Rollout: Bounding How Much Traffic a Mistake Reaches ¶4
results.finding: The three cadences are introduced in three different sentence shapes ('One team's, from 2021', 'And payment terminals, whose...', 'For the platform'); both readers had to count back to find the three.

results.draft_locus: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
results.quote: That last point is my recommendation, drawn from this book's test for a single payment
results.finding: The test is referred to here but only stated later in the takeaways ('an answer is a promise until a later record confirms it'); both readers could not resolve the reference at this point.

results.draft_locus: Incidents, Postmortems and the Engineering Choices Behind Them ¶1
results.quote: both about a denial-of-service attack on 21 April 2025
results.finding: flow-A: a denial-of-service attack is not a change, so Adyen's only public incident account does not fit a chapter about change. The spec selects this evidence for postmortem practice; the draft does not say that it is cited only to show publication practice, not as a change.

results.draft_locus: Why a Money Path Cannot Stop Changing, and What a Bad Change Costs ¶2
results.quote: The second reason is that a rarer release is a larger one.
results.finding: flow-B: the paragraph announces two reasons, the first grows into a long passage on freezes, and the second arrives so late the reader had to look back for the first.

results.draft_locus: Four Ways to Limit a Change, and What Each Costs ¶1
results.quote: Its second column of gaps ends the same way in every row.
results.finding: flow-B: the gaps column ('What it cannot catch') is not the second column, the release-window row says 'Anything' rather than ending the same way, and 'four designs' then 'a fifth step' mixes terms.

results.quote: a change reached 1% of what Stripe calls its critical tier of traffic
results.finding: 'Critical tier' is not in already_knows and is used from the first paragraph; only much later does the draft admit Stripe does not define it. Saying so at first use would stop readers searching for a missed definition. ('The books' and 'the edge' were also flagged by both readers, but they come from an earlier Part VIII chapter the audience already knows, so they are not failed.)

The introduction opens from the previous chapter's near miss into a dated, numbered incident (8 February 2024, 39/15/12 failed payments); no dictionary opening, sweeping generalisation or throat-clearing.

The conclusion sorts what is established, what depends on context and the author's own position, then closes with an asymmetry and a concrete exercise; no bare restatement, apology or unanchored new claim. The part-level material is a spec-mandated callback (handled under flow).

Synthesis: the asymmetry between what providers document (what gives way) and what a merchant cannot verify. So-what: 'Your own reliability therefore rests on three things you can check' and the one-line exercise per money path, plus the rule that a change is finished when the records agree.

Calls back to the six minutes of 8 February 2024 ('failed payments for six minutes on 8 February 2024'; 'a rollout that got no further than one percent') and to the part opening's two Larkfield first-of-month runs (7,900 late renewals, 1,840 double charges, K5 and K1), as conclusion.callback declares.

The cold reader's predicted order matches the nine body sections exactly and the thesis, including the author's own reconciliation rule. Uncertainties (the four ways are not named; how the incidents section differs from the comparison) do not contradict the roadmap.

The reader says the incident is still open because 1% is real payments, gives Larkfield's ~5 / ~90 counts and the three states, and lists the four recovery steps (list by build, confirm with provider, compare with ledger, repair under the stored idempotency key) before closing, matching expected.

The reader orders: dark run comparing the finance export line by line, new version beside the old behind a per-customer flag, way back rehearsed, withdrawal signals, staged widening, and deletion of the old path only after a full reporting period reconciles. Matches expected; the reader does not mention a planned upgrade calendar, a secondary element.

No frequency comparison is made; the draft says why ('That counts releases of a system, and Stripe's 400 a day counts deployments to one service'; 'Deployment frequency is the one figure here that cannot even be compared'). Reconciliation after change is labelled the author's recommendation and the draft states 'Neither Stripe nor Adyen has published such a gate'.

What to Take Away ¶4 returns to the 1 October and 1 November 2026 runs and states 'the five chapters of this part show an asymmetry that none shows alone', naming what the providers document and what a merchant cannot verify.
